newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. firms in Kuwait take measures after threats.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms in Kuwait take measures after threats.

text.p: The U.S. embassy in Kuwait and some companies said on Monday they were taking new security precautions following reported threats against American interests in the Gulf Arab state.
But many Americans said there was no sense of alert among the community in Kuwait, where about 7,000 U.S. citizens live, including about 4,500 military personnel.
They said U.S. firms were alternating work hours or reducing the number of staff present at their premises at the same time.
The embassy on Sunday warned American citizens to exercise particular caution over the next few days in light of reported threats against U.S. interests in Kuwait.
It did not elaborate on the threats.
"I was told not to come to work today. I think it is an over-reaction to the threat," one American employee said.
"We have told our non-essential staff not to report to work today (Monday). We are taking some precautions," said an official at another U.S. company.
"The embassy is taking added security precautions," an embassy spokeswoman said. She refused to elaborate.

A ceremony planned for Monday at the embassy to commemorate U.S. servicemen who died in the 1991 Gulf War that ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait was postponed due to security concerns, the U.S. residents said.

The embassy has asked Americans to review their security arrangements and avoid predictable movements, vary routes and schedules, be wary of unexpected visitors or packages and inspect vehicles for any sign of tampering.
It also urged U.S. citizens to avoid actions that could draw attention to them and be alert to surveillance and "unusual or overly inquisitive persons or callers."
Any security concerns should be called to the embassy's attention, the embassy said in a public announcement.

Three people were killed and 59 were wounded on December 12, 1983 when a suicide bomber rammed a truck laden with 300 kg (660 pounds) of explosives into the U.S. embassy in one of eight attacks on U.S. interests in Kuwait that day.
Kuwaitis blamed those bombings on Iraqi opposition Shi'ite Moslems dmanding the creation of an Islamic state in Iraq.

The U.S. embassy in Kuwait had boosted its security since 19 U.S. airmen were killed in the bombing of a military housing complex in al-Khobar in neighbouring Saudi Arabia in June. Five Americans and two Indians were killed by a car bomb in the Saudi capital Riyadh last November.
